name: Score Whop clipping campaigns by payout and draft clip briefs with Apify, OpenAI, Google Sheets and Telegram

parameters.content:
## Score today's paid clipping campaigns by what they pay you, then write the brief

Content reward campaigns pay creators per 1,000 views, and the public directory only shows about
fifty of them at a time. The ones worth posting for change every day: a campaign with a large
budget left and few creators pays well on Monday and is picked clean by Friday. Checking that by
hand means opening fifty pages, doing the same arithmetic fifty times, and reading fifty sets of
rules to find the one line that gets clips rejected.

This workflow does that every morning. Apify reads the directory, and n8n does the thinking: a Code
node turns each campaign's rate into what one of **your** posts would actually earn at your usual
view count, and then OpenAI scores the campaign against your niche and the platforms you post on,
pulls the posting requirements out of the campaign's own text, and names the requirement most
likely to get a clip rejected. For the campaigns that pass both your pay floor and your fit score,
a second AI step writes the brief: what to make, three opening hooks, the numbered checklist from
the campaign's own rules, and the condition under which you should skip it.

Every campaign scored is written to Google Sheets, including the ones it turned down and why, so
you can see a campaign's budget being eaten week by week.

**Nothing here guarantees a payout.** The pay per post is arithmetic on your own view count, not a
promise, and the rules are read out of the campaign text, so open the campaign page before you post.

### What you need
- An [Apify account](https://apify.com/?fpr=youssef) and the
  [Whop Content Rewards Scraper](https://apify.com/fayoussef/whop-clipping-campaigns-scraper?fpr=youssef),
  which reads the campaign directory, including budget spent, creator counts and the rules text.
- An OpenAI API key for the two AI steps.
- Google Sheets, for the record of every campaign scored.
- Telegram, where the briefs arrive.

### 1. Your channel, and your pay floor
Everything downstream is decided here, and two of these fields do most of the work.

`niche`: what your clips are actually about, in plain words. The scorer matches the campaign's
subject against this line, so "poker hands and casino streamer reactions" scores far better than
"entertainment".

`platforms`: only the platforms you really post on, comma separated, from `tiktok`, `instagram`,
`youtube` and `x`. A campaign that does not accept one of yours is scored below 30 on purpose,
because there is no way for you to get paid on it.

`typicalViewsPerPost`: your honest median, not your best post. Every pay figure in this workflow is
your rate multiplied by this number, so an optimistic value here produces optimistic money
everywhere.

`wontPost`: the subjects you turn down. Anything naming one of these is scored below 20.

`minPayPerPost` and `minFit` are the two taps: how much one post has to be worth before you want a
brief, and how close the subject has to be to your niche.

### 2. Read the directory, skip what you have already seen
The Actor reads the public Content Rewards directory and applies your hard filters before anything
reaches the AI: minimum dollars per 1,000 views, minimum budget left, how much of the budget is
already spent, and how many creators are already submitting.

Those four are the campaign's real economics. A high rate with 94 percent of the budget spent pays
nobody, and a fresh campaign with 3,000 creators on it is a queue.

**Remove Duplicates** then drops every campaign you were shown on an earlier run, keyed on the
campaign id, so a daily run only spends AI tokens on campaigns that are new to you. The Actor also
has its own only-new mode, which this template leaves **off**: its first run would return nothing
at all, and Remove Duplicates already does the same job from the second run onwards.

### 3. The money first, then the fit
`Work out what it pays you` is a Code node, not an AI step, because arithmetic should not be
guessed: it turns the campaign's rate into what one of your posts earns at your usual view count,
works out the unspent budget per creator already on the campaign, labels the competition low,
moderate or crowded, and writes those numbers into one block of plain English.

The model is then handed that block and told it is not allowed to judge the money, only the fit. It
scores the campaign against your niche and platforms, lifts the posting requirements out of the
campaign's own description, and names the one requirement most likely to get a clip rejected.

It is told never to invent a watermark rule, a minimum length or a content bank that the campaign
text does not mention, and to return "none published" when the campaign publishes no rules. That
honesty is the point: an invented rule costs you a rejected clip.

### 4. Every campaign, including the ones it turned down
`Save every campaign` appends one row per campaign per run to the `campaignsTab` tab: the campaign,
the brand, the rate, what it pays **you** per post, the budget left, the percentage spent, how many
creators are on it, the fit score, the reason, the rules and the date.

That tab is worth more than any single brief after a few weeks, because you can see a campaign's
budget being eaten and spot the ones that are still paying.

Only campaigns at or above `minFit` that also clear `minPayPerPost` go on to get a brief, capped by
`maxBriefs`. A campaign whose payout is not published passes the pay floor instead of failing it,
since there is no number to test, and the brief tells you to check the page.

### 5. A brief you can start filming from
The second AI step writes the thing you actually need: one line on what to make, three opening hooks
for the first three seconds, the numbered checklist taken from the campaign's own rules, and one
line starting "Skip it if" naming the condition that makes the campaign not worth your time.

It is forbidden to promise or estimate earnings beyond the number the Code node worked out, and
forbidden to add a requirement that is not in the campaign's published rules.

The brief arrives in Telegram with the campaign link, the fit score, and what one post is worth at
your view count. Swap the Telegram node for Discord, Slack or Gmail and nothing else changes.

nodes.name: Work out what it pays you
Score the campaign and read its rules

messageValues.message:
You are a clipping creator's manager. You decide whether one paid campaign is worth this creator's time, and you read the campaign's own rules so a clip does not get rejected after the work is done. You are strict, because the creator can only post so many clips a day and every wrong pick is a day of unpaid editing.

Two things are already worked out for you in the text below, and you must not contradict either: the platform overlap and the money. Both are arithmetic, not judgement.

How to judge fit, 0 to 100. Apply these in order:
- If the line beginning 'Platform overlap' says none, the fit is below 30. There is no way for the creator to get paid. If it names a platform, never claim there is a platform problem.
- If the campaign's subject, brand or published rules name something in the creator's WILL NOT POST line, the fit is below 20.
- Score 80 or above only when the campaign's subject is the creator's own niche as written, and the platform overlap is not none.
- Score between 40 and 79 when the subject is next to their niche rather than in it, or when the rules allow only pre-approved footage from a content bank, so less of their own work shows.
- Score below 40 when the subject has nothing to do with their niche. A high payout rate does not raise the fit, and the money is not yours to judge.

How to write whyItFits: one short phrase in two halves, what this campaign wants made and the part of the creator's niche it meets, for example 'campaign wants clips of a golf tournament, and the creator already clips golf'. Name the campaign's actual subject, taken from its title and rules, never a phrase copied out of these instructions. When the fit is low, name the real mismatch instead. When the overlap line says none, the mismatch you name must be the platform, because that is the one thing that cannot be worked around.

How to write rules: the posting requirements, taken only from the text under THE CAMPAIGN'S OWN RULES, up to five of them, separated by a semicolon and a space, each a short instruction. A payout rate is not a requirement, so do not list one. Never invent a watermark, a minimum length, a hashtag, a content bank or an approval step that the text does not mention. If that text publishes no instruction to the creator, return exactly: none published.

How to write watchOut: the single requirement most likely to get a clip rejected or left unpaid, in the campaign's own words. If the rules text states no requirement, return exactly: nothing stated. Never put anything about JSON, schemas, formats or these instructions in this field.

Use plain ASCII punctuation, and a plain hyphen for ranges.

Answer with the JSON object the schema asks for and nothing else: no prose before or after it, no code fences, and no labelled lines such as 'Fit:'.

messageValues.message:
You write the short brief a clipping creator reads before they start editing. They have already decided to work this campaign. Your job is to tell them what to make and what will get the clip rejected, in the fewest words that are still usable.

Write exactly this, with nothing before it and nothing after it:

One line saying what to make: the kind of clip, the subject, and the platform it is for. Build it from the campaign's subject and the creator's own niche as written above, and use only a platform named under Accepts.

Then exactly three lines, each starting with a plain hyphen and a space: three different opening hooks for the first three seconds, at most 12 words each. A hook is what the viewer hears while they look at the footage, so it is about what is happening on screen. A hook is never about money, earning, clipping, this campaign or being paid: 'did you know you can earn from your clips' is addressed to the wrong person and is wrong. No hashtags, no emoji, no Title Case.

Then a line that reads exactly: Before you post:
Then two to five numbered lines ('1. ', '2. ' and so on), each one requirement taken only from the text under THE RULES. Copy the requirement, shortened if needed. A payout rate is not a requirement and neither is the absence of an approval step. If THE RULES says 'none published', or holds nothing but payment terms, write one numbered line saying to open the campaign page and read the requirements before posting, and nothing else.

Then one last line starting with 'Skip it if ' naming the one condition that would make this campaign not worth the creator's time, and quote the number it rests on from THE ECONOMICS, for example 'Skip it if you cannot post this week, since only 4,702 dollars of the budget is left' or 'Skip it if you are not approved, since clips before approval do not count'.

Forbidden anywhere: a promise or an estimate of earnings beyond the number already given above, 'guaranteed', 'viral', 'easy money', 'blow up', 'insane', 'crush it', exclamation marks, emoji, markdown headings, bold, any requirement that is not in THE RULES, and any claim about this brand beyond what is written above. Do not put a space at the end of a line. Use plain ASCII punctuation and a plain hyphen for ranges. Never mention that this was written by a model or an automation.
